danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 32
paragraphs: Der var gået syv dage, siden fyrst Andrej befandt sig på forbindingspladsen ved Borodinó. Hans febrile tilstand og betændelsen i hans indvolde, som var beskadiget, ville efter lægens mening med sikkerhed tage livet af ham. Men på den syvende dag spiste han med fornøjelse et stykke brød med lidt te, og lægen bemærkede, at hans feber var faldet. Han havde genvundet bevidstheden den morgen. Den første nat efter afrejsen fra Moskva havde været forholdsvis varm, og han var blevet i kalèchen, men ved Mytísjtji bad den sårede selv om at blive båret ud og få lidt te. Smerterne ved flytningen ind i hytten havde fået ham til at stønne højt og miste bevidstheden igen. Da han var blevet lagt på sin feltseng, lå han længe ubevægelig med lukkede øjne. Så åbnede han dem og hviskede sagte: »Og teen?« At han huskede en så lille dagligdags detalje, forbløffede lægen. Han følte fyrst Andrejs puls og konstaterede til sin overraskelse og utilfredshed, at den var bedret. Han var utilfreds, fordi han af erfaring vidste, at hvis patienten ikke døde nu, ville han gøre det lidt senere under endnu større lidelser. Timókhin, den rødnæsede major fra fyrst Andrejs regiment, havde sluttet sig til ham i Moskva og blev transporteret sammen med ham, såret i benet ved Borodinó. De blev ledsaget af en læge, fyrst Andrejs kammertjener, hans kusk og to ordonnanser.
De gav fyrst Andrej noget te. Han drak den ivrigt og så med febrilske øjne mod døren foran sig, som forsøgte han at forstå og huske noget.
»Jeg vil ikke have mere. Er Timókhin her?« spurgte han.
Timókhin krøb langs bænken hen til ham.
»Jeg er her, Deres excellence.«
»Hvordan er dit sår?«
»Mit, hr.? Helt fint. Men hvordan har De det?«
Fyrst Andrej grublede igen, som forsøgte han at huske noget.
»Kunne man ikke skaffe en bog?« spurgte han.
»Hvilken bog?«
»Evangelierne. Jeg har ikke et eksemplar.«

Lægen lovede at skaffe den til ham og begyndte at spørge, hvordan han havde det. Fyrst Andrej besvarede alle spørgsmålene modvilligt men fornuftigt og sagde derefter, at han gerne ville have en pude lagt under sig, for han lå ubekvemt og havde stærke smerter. Lægen og kammertjeneren løftede kappen, han var tildækket med, og grimaserede over den modbydelige lugt af forrådnet kød fra såret, mens de undersøgte det forfærdelige sted. Lægen var meget utilfreds med noget og foretog en ændring i forbindingerne, hvorved de vendte den sårede om, så han atter stønnede og blev bevidstløs og vildrede i feber af smerte. Han blev ved med at bede dem om at hente bogen og lægge den under ham.
»Hvad besvær ville det være for jer?« sagde han. »Jeg har den ikke. Vær rar at skaffe mig den og lægge den under et øjeblik,« bad han med klagende stemme.
Lægen gik ud i gangen for at vaske hænder.

»I har ingen samvittighed,« sagde han til kammertjeneren, der hældte vand over hans hænder. »Bare et øjeblik så jeg ikke på dig... Det gør så ondt, forstår du, at jeg undrer mig over, at han kan holde det ud.«
»Ved Vorherre Jesus Kristus, jeg troede, vi havde lagt noget under ham!« sagde kammertjeneren.

Den første gang fyrst Andrej forstod, hvor han var, og hvad der fejlede ham, og huskede, at han var såret, og hvordan det var gået til, var da han bad om at blive båret ind i hytten, efter at kalèchen havde holdt ved Mytísjtji. Efter at have mistet orienteringen af smerte under transporten til hytten genvandt han bevidstheden, og mens han drak te, mindedes han atter alt, hvad der var hændt, og frem for alt huskede han tydeligt øjeblikket på forbindingspladsen, hvor synet af en mands lidelser — en mand han ikke brød sig om — havde vakt de nye tanker i ham, som lovede ham lykke. Og disse tanker, skønt nu vage og ubestemte, fyldte atter hans sjæl. Han huskede, at han nu havde en ny kilde til lykke, og at denne lykke havde noget at gøre med evangelierne. Derfor bad han om et eksemplar. Den ubekvemme stilling, de havde lagt ham i og vendt ham til, forvirrede igen hans tanker, og da han kom til sig selv for tredje gang, var det i nattens fuldstændige stilhed. Alle omkring ham sov. En fårekylling sang fra den anden side af gangen; nogen råbte og sang ude på gaden; kakerlakker raslede på bordet, på ikonerne og på væggene, og en stor flue summede ved hovedgærdet og omkring lyset ved siden af ham, hvis væge var forkullet og havde formet sig som en svamp.

Hans sind var ikke i normal tilstand. Et sundt menneske tænker, føler og husker normalt utallige ting på én gang, men har evnen og viljen til at vælge én tankerække eller begivenhedsrække at samle hele sin opmærksomhed om. Et sundt menneske kan rive sig løs fra de dybeste overvejelser for at sige et venligt ord til en, der kommer ind, og derefter vende tilbage til sine egne tanker. Men fyrst Andrejs sind var ikke i normal tilstand i den henseende. Alle hans åndelige evner var mere aktive og klare end nogensinde, men de virkede uafhængigt af hans vilje. De mest forskellige tanker og billeder optog ham samtidig. Til tider begyndte hans hjerne pludselig at arbejde med en kraft, klarhed og dybde, den aldrig havde nået, da han var rask, men midt i arbejdet drejede den pludselig hen på en uventet tanke, og han havde ikke kræfter til at bringe den tilbage.

»Ja, en ny lykke blev åbenbaret for mig, som mennesket ikke kan fratages,« tænkte han, mens han lå i halvmørket i den stille hytte og stirrede stift frem for sig med febrisk vidtåbne øjne. »En lykke hinsides materielle kræfter, uden for de materielle påvirkninger, der virker på mennesket — sjælens lykke alene, kærlighedens lykke. Ethvert menneske kan forstå den, men at udtænke den og foreskrive den var kun muligt for Gud. Men hvordan foreskrev Gud den lov? Og hvorfor Sønnen...?«

Og pludselig brød denne tankerække af, og fyrst Andrej hørte (uden at vide om det var en hallucination eller virkelighed) en blid hvisken, der uophørligt og rytmisk gentog »piti-piti-piti« og så »titi« og så igen »piti-piti-piti« og »ti-ti« endnu engang. Samtidig følte han, at over hans ansigt, lige midt over det, rejste sig en underlig luftig konstruktion af slanke nåle eller splinter til lyden af denne hviskede musik. Han følte, at han måtte balancere forsigtigt (skønt det var vanskeligt), så denne luftige konstruktion ikke styrtede sammen; men alligevel styrtede den stadig sammen og rejste sig atter langsomt til lyden af den hviskede rytmiske musik — »den strækker sig, strækker sig, breder sig ud og strækker sig,« sagde fyrst Andrej til sig selv. Mens han lyttede til denne hvisken og mærkede fornemmelsen af denne udstrækning og opbygningen af dette nålebyggeri, så han også glimt af en rød glorie omkring lyset og hørte kakerlakkernes raslen og summen af fluen, der daskede mod hans pude og ansigt. Hver gang fluen rørte hans ansigt, gav den ham en brændende fornemmelse, og dog ødelagde den til hans overraskelse ikke konstruktionen, skønt den ramte netop det område af hans ansigt, hvor den rejste sig. Men ud over dette var der noget andet vigtigt. Det var noget hvidt ved døren — statuen af en sfinks, som også tyngede ham.

»Men måske er det min skjorte på bordet,« tænkte han, »og dér er mine ben, og dér er døren, men hvorfor strækker den sig altid ud og trækker sig ud, og 'piti-piti-piti' og 'ti-ti' og 'piti-piti-piti'...? Nu er det nok, hold venligst op!« bønfaldt fyrst Andrej smertefuldt nogen. Og pludselig svømmede tanker og følelser igen op til overfladen af hans sind med særlig klarhed og kraft.

»Ja — kærlighed,« tænkte han igen helt klart. »Men ikke kærlighed, der elsker for noget, for en egenskab, for et formål eller af en grund, men den kærlighed, som jeg — døende — først erfarede, da jeg så min fjende og alligevel elskede ham. Jeg erfarede den følelse af kærlighed, som er selve sjælens væsen og ikke kræver et objekt. Nu føler jeg atter den salighed. At elske sin næste, at elske sine fjender, at elske alt, at elske Gud i alle hans tilkendegivelser. Det er muligt at elske et kært menneske med menneskelig kærlighed, men en fjende kan kun elskes med guddommelig kærlighed. Derfor erfarede jeg den glæde, da jeg følte, at jeg elskede den mand. Hvad er der blevet af ham? Er han i live?...«

»Når man elsker med menneskelig kærlighed, kan man gå fra kærlighed til had, men guddommelig kærlighed kan ikke forandres. Nej, hverken døden eller noget andet kan ødelægge den. Den er selve sjælens væsen. Og dog, hvor mange mennesker har jeg ikke hadet i mit liv? Og af dem alle elskede og hadede jeg ingen som hende.« Og han forestillede sig levende Natasja, ikke som han havde gjort det før, med kun hendes ynde, der glædede ham, men for første gang forestillede han sig hendes sjæl. Og han forstod hendes følelser, hendes lidelser, skam og anger. Han forstod nu for første gang hele grusomheden i sit afslag, grusomheden i sit brud med hende. »Bare det var muligt at se hende endnu engang! Bare én gang, at se ind i de øjne og sige...«

»Piti-piti-piti og ti-ti og piti-piti-piti bum!« daskede fluen.... Og hans opmærksomhed blev pludselig ført ind i en anden verden, en verden af virkelighed og delirium, hvor noget bestemt foregik. I den verden rejste en konstruktion sig stadig og faldt ikke, noget strakte sig stadig ud, og lyset med sin røde glorie brændte endnu, og den samme skjorteagtige sfinks lå nær døren; men ud over alt dette knirkede noget, der kom et pust af frisk luft, og en ny hvid sfinks dukkede op, stående ved døren. Og den sfinks havde det blege ansigt og de skinnende øjne som tilhørte netop den Natasja, han lige havde tænkt på.

»Åh, hvor dette evindelige delirium er trykkende,« tænkte fyrst Andrej og forsøgte at jage ansigtet fra sin fantasi. Men ansigtet forblev foran ham med virkelighedens kraft og nærmede sig. Fyrst Andrej ønskede at vende tilbage til den forrige verden af ren tanke, men han kunne ikke, og deliriet trak ham tilbage til sit rige. Den bløde hviskende stemme fortsatte sin rytmiske mumlen, noget trykkede ham og strakte sig ud, og det fremmede ansigt var foran ham. Fyrst Andrej samlede al sin styrke i et forsøg på at genvinde sin bevidsthed, han rørte sig en smule, og pludselig ringede det for hans ører, der blev mørkt for hans øjne, og som en mand, der kastes i vandet, mistede han bevidstheden. Da han kom til sig selv, var Natasja, den samme levende Natasja, som han af alle mennesker mest længtes efter at elske med denne nye rene guddommelige kærlighed, der var blevet åbenbaret for ham, knælende foran ham. Han indså, at det var den virkelige levende Natasja, og han blev ikke overrasket men stille lykkelig. Natasja, ubevægelig på sine knæ (hun var ude af stand til at røre sig), med forskræmte øjne naglet til ham, holdt sine hulk tilbage. Hendes ansigt var blegt og stift. Kun i den nederste del skælvede noget.
Fyrst Andrej åndede lettet, smilede og rakte hånden frem.
»Dig?« sagde han. »Hvilken lykke!«
Med en hurtig men forsigtig bevægelse rykkede Natasja nærmere på sine knæ og tog forsigtigt hans hånd, bøjede ansigtet over den og begyndte at kysse den, idet hun knapt rørte den med læberne.
»Tilgiv mig!« hviskede hun og løftede hovedet for at se på ham. »Tilgiv mig!«
»Jeg elsker dig,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
»Tilgiv...!«
»Tilgive hvad?« spurgte han.
»Tilgiv mig for hvad jeg ha-r gjo-rt!« stammede Natasja i en knap hørlig, brudt hvisken og begyndte at kysse hans hånd hurtigere, idet hun knapt berørte den med læberne.
»Jeg elsker dig mere, bedre end før,« sagde fyrst Andrej og løftede hendes ansigt med hånden for at se hende i øjnene.

De øjne, fyldt med lykkelige tårer, så på ham sky, medfølende og med glædesfyldt kærlighed. Natasjas tynde blege ansigt med de opsvulmede læber var mere end uskønt — det var skrækkeligt. Men fyrst Andrej så det ikke, han så hendes strålende øjne, som var smukke. De hørte lyden af stemmer bag sig.

Kammertjeneren Peter, som nu var helt vågen, havde vækket lægen. Timókhin, der slet ikke havde sovet på grund af smerterne i benet, havde længe iagttaget alt, hvad der foregik, mens han omhyggeligt tildækkede sin bare krop med lagenet, sammenkrøbet på sin bænk.
»Hvad er det her?« sagde lægen, da han rejste sig fra sengen. »Vær venlig at gå, frue!«
I det øjeblik bankede en stuepige, sendt af grevinden, der havde bemærket sin datters fravær, på døren.
Som en søvngænger, der vækkes af sin søvn, gik Natasja ud af værelset og faldt grædende på sin seng, da hun kom tilbage til sin hytte.

Fra den tid, under hele resten af Rostov-familiens rejse, ved hvert opholdssted og overalt, hvor de overnattede, forlod Natasja aldrig den sårede Bolkonskij, og lægen måtte indrømme, at han ikke havde forventet hverken en sådan fasthed eller en sådan dygtighed i at pleje en såret mand af en ung pige.

Hvor forfærdeligt grevinden end forestillede sig, at det ville være, hvis fyrst Andrej døde i hendes datters arme under rejsen — og efter hvad lægen sagde, syntes det let at kunne ske — kunne hun ikke modsætte sig Natasja. Skønt tanken med det nære forhold mellem den sårede mand og Natasja forekom, at deres tidligere forlovelse ville blive fornyet, hvis han kom sig, talte ingen — og mindst af alle Natasja og fyrst Andrej — om dette: det uafklarede spørgsmål om liv og død, der hang ikke blot over Bolkonskij men over hele Rusland, udelukkede alle andre overvejelser.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 32
paragraphs: Seven days had gone by since Prince Andrew had found himself at the dressing station on the field of Borodino. In the doctor's opinion, his fever and the inflammation of his injured bowels were sure to kill him. But on the seventh day he ate a piece of bread with tea and enjoyed it, and the doctor saw that his temperature was lower. He had come to his senses that morning. The first night after they left Moscow had been fairly warm, so he had stayed in the calèche. At Mytishchi, though, the wounded man himself asked to be taken out and given some tea. Being carried into the hut hurt so much that he groaned aloud and lost consciousness again. Once they had laid him on his camp bed, he lay motionless with his eyes shut for a long time. Then he opened them and whispered: "And the tea?" The doctor was astonished that he remembered such a small detail of daily life. He felt Prince Andrew's pulse and found, to his surprise and annoyance, that it was better. He was annoyed because experience had taught him that if the patient did not die now, he would die a little later and suffer more. Timokhin, the red-nosed major of Prince Andrew's regiment, had joined him in Moscow and was being taken along with him, wounded in the leg at Borodino. With them traveled a doctor, Prince Andrew's valet, his coachman and two orderlies.
They gave Prince Andrew some tea. He drank it eagerly, his feverish eyes fixed on the door in front of him, as if he were trying to understand and remember something.
"I don't want any more. Is Timokhin here?" he asked.
Timokhin crawled along the bench toward him.
"I'm here, your excellency."
"How is your wound?"
"Mine, sir? It's all right. But how are you?"
Prince Andrew again grew thoughtful, as if trying to remember something.
"Could someone find me a book?" he asked.
"What book?"
"The Gospels. I don't have one."

The doctor promised to get it for him and began asking how he felt. Prince Andrew answered every question reluctantly but sensibly. Then he said he wanted a bolster under him, because he was uncomfortable and in great pain. The doctor and the valet lifted the cloak that covered him. They made faces at the foul smell of rotting flesh from the wound and began examining that dreadful place. Something displeased the doctor very much, and he changed the dressings. He turned the wounded man over, and Prince Andrew groaned again, and the agony made him lose consciousness and rave. He kept asking them to get him the book and put it under him.
"What trouble would it be for you?" he said. "I don't have one. Please get it and put it under me for a moment," he begged in a pitiful voice.
The doctor went out into the passage to wash his hands.
"You fellows have no conscience," he said to the valet, who was pouring water over his hands. "I took my eyes off you for one moment... The pain is so bad, you know, that I wonder how he bears it."
"By the Lord Jesus Christ, I thought we'd put something under him!" said the valet.

The first time Prince Andrew understood where he was and what was wrong with him, and remembered that he was wounded and how, was when he asked to be carried into the hut after his calèche stopped at Mytishchi. Pain had confused him while he was carried in, but he came to again. While he drank his tea he recalled everything that had happened to him. Above all he remembered vividly the moment at the dressing station when, seeing the suffering of a man he disliked, those new thoughts had come to him that promised him happiness. Those thoughts, though vague and indistinct now, took hold of his soul again. He remembered that he now had a new source of happiness, and that this happiness had something to do with the Gospels. That was why he had asked for a copy. But the awkward position they had put him in, and the turning over, had muddled his thoughts again. When he came to himself a third time, it was in the complete stillness of the night. Everyone near him was asleep. A cricket chirped across the passage, and someone in the street was shouting and singing. Cockroaches rustled on the table, on the icons and on the walls. A big fly flopped about at the head of the bed and around the candle beside him, whose charred wick had curled into the shape of a mushroom.

His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy man usually thinks of, feels and remembers countless things at once. Yet he has the power and the will to pick one train of thoughts or events and fix his whole attention on it. A healthy man can tear himself away from his deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who comes in, and then go back to his own thoughts. In that respect Prince Andrew's mind was not normal. All its powers were more active and clearer than ever, but they worked apart from his will. The most varied thoughts and images filled his mind at the same time. At moments his brain suddenly worked with a vigor, clarity and depth it had never reached when he was well. Then, in the middle of that work, it would veer off to some unexpected idea, and he had no strength to turn it back.

"Yes, a new happiness was revealed to me, one that man cannot be deprived of," he thought, as he lay in the half-darkness of the quiet hut, staring ahead with wide, feverish eyes. "A happiness that lies beyond material forces, outside the material influences that act on a man — a happiness of the soul alone, the happiness of loving. Every man can understand it, but only God could conceive it and command it. But how did God command that law? And why was the Son...?"

And suddenly this train of thought broke off. Prince Andrew heard (without knowing whether it was delusion or reality) a soft whispering voice repeating over and over, in a steady rhythm, "piti-piti-piti," then "titi," and then "piti-piti-piti" again, and "ti-ti" once more. At the same time he felt that above his face, right over its middle, some strange airy structure of slender needles or splinters was being built, to the sound of this whispered music. He felt he had to balance carefully (though it was hard) to keep this airy structure from collapsing. Yet it kept collapsing and slowly rising again to the sound of the whispered rhythmic music. "It stretches, stretches, spreading out and stretching," Prince Andrew said to himself. As he listened to the whispering and felt this drawing out and the building of the edifice of needles, he also saw, in glimpses, a red halo around the candle. He heard the rustle of the cockroaches and the buzzing of the fly that flopped against his pillow and his face. Each time the fly touched his face it burned him, and yet, to his surprise, it did not destroy the structure, though it struck the very spot on his face where the structure was rising. But there was something else of importance too. It was something white by the door — the statue of a sphinx, which also weighed on him.

"But perhaps that's my shirt on the table," he thought, "and that's my legs, and that's the door. But why does it keep stretching and drawing itself out, and 'piti-piti-piti' and 'ti-ti' and 'piti-piti-piti'...? That's enough, please stop!" Prince Andrew begged someone in anguish. And suddenly thoughts and feelings rose again to the surface of his mind with remarkable clarity and force.

"Yes — love," he thought again, quite clearly. "But not the love that loves for something, for some quality, some purpose or some reason. It's the love I first felt, while dying, when I saw my enemy and still loved him. I felt that love which is the very essence of the soul and needs no object. Now I feel that bliss again. To love your neighbors, to love your enemies, to love everything, to love God in all His forms. You can love someone dear to you with human love, but an enemy can be loved only with divine love. That is why I felt such joy when I realized that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?...

"When you love with human love, you can pass from love to hatred, but divine love cannot change. No, neither death nor anything else can destroy it. It is the very essence of the soul. And yet how many people I have hated in my life! Of them all, there was none I loved and hated as I did her." And he pictured Natasha vividly. He no longer saw only her charms, which had delighted him before. For the first time he pictured her soul. And he understood her feelings, her suffering, her shame and remorse. For the first time he understood how cruel it had been to reject her, how cruel his break with her. "If only I could see her once more! Just once, to look into those eyes and say..."

"Piti-piti-piti and ti-ti and piti-piti-piti boom!" the fly flopped.... And his attention was suddenly carried into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something peculiar was happening. In that world some structure was still going up and had not fallen, something was still stretching out, and the candle with its red halo was still burning, and the same shirtlike sphinx lay by the door. But besides all this, something creaked, a breath of fresh air came in, and a new white sphinx appeared, standing at the door. And that sphinx had the pale face and shining eyes of the very Natasha he had just been thinking about.

"Oh, how oppressive this endless delirium is," thought Prince Andrew, trying to drive that face out of his imagination. But the face stayed in front of him with the force of reality and came nearer. Prince Andrew wanted to return to that earlier world of pure thought, but he couldn't, and the delirium drew him back into its realm. The soft whispering voice went on with its rhythmic murmur, something weighed on him and stretched out, and the strange face was in front of him. Prince Andrew gathered all his strength to recover his senses. He moved a little, and suddenly his ears rang, his eyes dimmed, and like a man plunged into water he lost consciousness. When he came to himself, Natasha was kneeling in front of him — that same living Natasha whom, of all people, he most longed to love with this new, pure, divine love that had been revealed to him. He realized that it was the real, living Natasha, and he was not surprised but quietly happy. Natasha knelt motionless (she could not stir), her frightened eyes fixed on him, holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and rigid. Only in its lower part did something quiver.
Prince Andrew sighed with relief, smiled and held out his hand.
"You?" he said. "How fortunate!"
Quickly but carefully, Natasha moved closer to him on her knees. She took his hand gently, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.
"Forgive me!" she whispered, raising her head and glancing at him. "Forgive me!"
"I love you," said Prince Andrew.
"Forgive...!"
"Forgive what?" he asked.
"Forgive me for what I ha-ve do-ne!" Natasha faltered in a broken, scarcely audible whisper, and she kissed his hand faster, just touching it with her lips.
"I love you more, and better, than before," said Prince Andrew, lifting her face with his hand so that he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, full of happy tears, looked at him timidly, with compassion and joyful love. Natasha's thin, pale face, with its swollen lips, was more than plain — it was dreadful. But Prince Andrew didn't see that. He saw her shining eyes, which were beautiful. Behind them they heard voices.

Peter the valet, now wide awake, had roused the doctor. Timokhin had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg. He had been watching everything for a long time, huddled on his bench and carefully covering his bare body with the sheet.
"What's this?" said the doctor, getting up from his bed. "Please go away, madam!"
At that moment a maid knocked at the door. The countess had sent her, having noticed that her daughter was missing.
Like a sleepwalker woken from her sleep, Natasha left the room. She went back to her hut and fell sobbing on her bed.

From then on, for the whole rest of the Rostovs' journey, at every halt and wherever they spent the night, Natasha never left the wounded Bolkonski. The doctor had to admit that he had not expected such firmness or such skill in nursing a wounded man from a young girl.

The countess imagined how dreadful it would be if Prince Andrew died in her daughter's arms during the journey — and, judging by what the doctor said, that might easily happen — but she could not oppose Natasha. A closeness had now grown up between the wounded man and Natasha, and it crossed her mind that if he recovered, their former engagement would be renewed. Still, no one spoke of this, least of all Natasha and Prince Andrew. The unsettled question of life and death, which hung not only over Bolkonski but over all Russia, shut out every other consideration.
